title: An Introductory Course to Judgment Aggregation
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1607.03307v1
published: 2016-07-12T10:57:30Z
summary: Reaching some form of consensus is often necessary for autonomous agents that want to coordinate their actions or otherwise engage in joint activities. One way to reach a consensus is by aggregating individual information, such as decisions, beliefs, preferences and constraints. Judgment aggregation is a social choice method, which generalises voting, that studies the aggregation of individual judgments regarding the truth-value of logically related propositions. As such, judgment aggregation is applicable for consensus reaching problems in multi agent systems. As other social choice theory, judgment aggregation research is abundant with impossibility results. However, the aim of this tutorial is to give an introduction to the methods of judgment aggregation, not the impossibility results. In particular, the tutorial will introduce the basic frameworks that model judgment aggregation problems and give an overview of the judgment aggregation functions so far developed as well as their social theoretic and computational complexity properties. The focus of the tutorial are consensus reaching problems in multi agent systems that can be modelled as judgment aggregation problems. Decisions Already Made
Ayoub Merimi and Souhail Bakkali and Abdeljalil Sakat
Abstract
Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the mo-
ment it is made; the action it commits to is la-
tent, carried out later, in a changing world. We
therefore introduce a timestamp theory of deci-
sion validity and a decision ledger that realises
it. Six timestamps define a decision; a fresh-
ness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence
guarantees at action time, placing the remain-
ing risk in information published afterwards.
Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities:
routing, which delivers that information to af-
fected decisions before their revision deadlines,
and temporal judgment, which reads it for the
time of action. The ledger is persistent state
holding each decision’s times, evidence and
background knowledge, indexed by watch con-
ditions written at decision time. Controlled
decision streams with exact labels confirm four
predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to fron-
tier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the
accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on de-
cisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows
routing; the ledger’s index sets what routing
reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect
dependencies at low exposure; and the remain-
ing errors concern when a change takes effect.
Freshness makes a decision right when it is
made; routing and temporal judgment keep it
right when it is carried out.
